paper_sections.title: Diagnostic, parent report data, and task performance

description.value: This study compared neural activation during reward and frustration in children with clinically high irritability and healthy children using a child-friendly frustration-induction task during fMRI. It also examined dimensional associations between parent-reported irritability and activation.

spans.text: This study assessed brain activation during reward and frustration, domains of behavioral deficits in childhood irritability.

description.value: Non-randomized, parallel-group, cross-sectional comparison of clinically irritable children and healthy comparison children; fMRI scanning occurred during the FETCH task.

spans.text: We conducted an fMRI investigation in children who were undergoing clinical treatment for severe irritability and a comparison group of healthy children.

description.value: Functional data were preprocessed, co-registered to Talairach-transformed anatomical images, and scrubbed for excessive movement before statistical analysis.

spans.text: Preprocessing included slice time correction (cubic spline interpolation), alignment of slice (cubic spline interpolation to the first non-discarded scan time), 3-dimensional motion correction (tri-linear interpolation), spatial smoothing (6 mm Gaussian kernel), linear trend removal, and temporal high-pass filtering (fast-Fourier transform based with a cutoff of 3 cycles/time course). During fMRI scanning, participants completed the Frustrative Emotion Task for Children (FETCH), which has been used previously to induce frustration in preschool and school age children ( Perlman et al., 2014 ).

description.value: Child-friendly negative mood induction task in which participants competed with Sparky to fetch bones by pressing a button, with win and lose trials grouped to induce positive and negative mood.

spans.text: In the task, subjects competed with Sparky, “a very sneaky dog”, to fetch bones by pressing a button as soon as the bone appeared on the screen
Win trials were indicated by an animated line drawing portraying the child grabbing the bone and placing it within one of the prize boxes during the feedback period

description.value: Trials in which the child fetched the bone before Sparky and received positive feedback.

spans.text: sometimes the child could fetch the bone before Sparky (win trials)
lose trials

description.value: Trials in which Sparky fetched the bone before the child's possible reaction time and provided negative feedback.

spans.text: sometimes the dog would fetch the bone before the child's possible reaction time (lose trials)
We analyzed this task using an event-related analytical design with all win trials as part of the win condition and all lose trials as part of the lose condition.

instructions.value: Press a button as soon as the bone appeared on the screen and try to fetch bones before Sparky.
